traps.snippet:
SELECT c.claim_id,
               c.claim_number,
               UPPER(RTRIM(c.lob_code)) AS lob_code,
               c.reported_date
        INTO   #open_claims
        FROM   stg.claims AS c WITH (NOLOCK)
        WHERE  c.status IN ('OPEN', 'REOPENED')
          AND  c.reported_date <= @AsOfDate;
traps.note: The #open_claims temp table becomes a DataFrame.
status is VARCHAR(12). Under the CI collation, IN ('OPEN','REOPENED') also matches 'Open' and 'reopened'. Spark's isin is case-sensitive and would drop those claims.
status is VARCHAR. Values stored with trailing spaces, such as 'OPEN ', still match in SQL Server but not with an exact match in Spark.

traps.snippet:
CREATE TABLE #aging (
            claim_id             INT            NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
            n_payments           INT            NOT NULL,
            total_paid           DECIMAL(14,2)  NULL,
            last_payment_date    DATE           NULL,
            last_activity_date   DATE    …
traps.note: The #aging temp table is filled row by row and becomes a DataFrame.
The claim_cur cursor loop handles one claim at a time and inserts into #aging. It becomes a set-based left join and aggregation per claim.

traps.snippet:
DECLARE pay_cur CURSOR LOCAL FAST_FORWARD FOR
                SELECT payment_date, amount
                FROM   #pay
                WHERE  claim_id = @claim_id
                ORDER  BY payment_date, payment_id;

            OPEN pay_cur;
            FETCH NEXT FROM pay_cur INTO @pay_date, @amoun…
traps.note: The nested pay_cur loop carries n_pay, total and last_pay from row to row in payment_date, payment_id order. It becomes count, sum and max per claim. Claims with no payments must get n_payments=0, total_paid=0 (not NULL) and last_payment_date NULL.

Latent: amount is nullable. One NULL amount makes @total NULL for the rest of that claim's loop and in the output, while Spark's sum skips NULLs. n_pay still counts that row. last_pay is the date of the last payment in order, which equals the max payment_date.
DATEDIFF(DAY) on DATE values is the plain day difference, so the value is safe. But Spark's datediff(end, start) takes its arguments in reverse order.
DATEDIFF(WEEK) counts the Sundays crossed between reported_date and @AsOfDate, not elapsed weeks. floor(datediff/7) would be wrong.

contracts.grain: One row per open or re-opened claim notified on or before the reporting date (@AsOfDate), aged on the days since its last payment up to that date, or since its reported date if nothing has been paid.

columns.name: n_payments
columns.description: Count of payments dated on or before @AsOfDate; 0 when there are none.

columns.name: total_paid
columns.description: Running sum that starts at 0, so it is 0 (not NULL) when there are no payments. If any payment amount is NULL the sum becomes NULL, which explains the 23 NULLs.

columns.name: last_payment_date
columns.description: Date of the last payment on or before @AsOfDate, taken from the last row when payments are ordered by payment_date then payment_id. NULL when there are no payments.

columns.name: weeks_open
columns.description: T-SQL DATEDIFF(WEEK, reported_date, as_of_date): counts how many week boundaries (Sundays) fall between the two dates, not days divided by 7.

columns.name: aging_band
columns.description: '0-29' when days < 30, '31-60' for 31-60, '61+' when days > 60. Because of a legacy gap, days = 30 falls through to 'UNKNOWN'.

columns.name: as_of_date
columns.description: The @AsOfDate parameter of the run. It is the same on every row.

defects.title: Ageing band gap: 30 days falls into UNKNOWN
defects.description: The band CASE uses @days < 30 for '0-29' and BETWEEN 31 AND 60 for '31-60'. A claim with exactly 30 days since last activity matches neither and gets 'UNKNOWN'. days_since_activity is never negative (reported_date <= AsOfDate and payment_date <= AsOfDate), so 30 is the only value that reaches UNKNOWN.
defects.intended_behaviour: The bands should cover every value with no gaps: 0-29, 30-60, 61+ (or 0-30, 31-60, 61+). Day 30 should get a real band, not UNKNOWN.
defects.impact_query: SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_affected FROM golden_rpt_claim_aging WHERE days_since_activity = 30 OR aging_band = 'UNKNOWN'

impact.query: SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_affected FROM golden_rpt_claim_aging WHERE days_since_activity = 30 OR aging_band = 'UNKNOWN'

defects.title: weeks_open counts week boundaries, not elapsed weeks
defects.description: weeks_open = DATEDIFF(WEEK, @reported, @AsOfDate). This counts the Sunday week boundaries crossed, not completed 7-day weeks, so a claim reported on a Saturday shows 1 week open the next day and the result can be one week off from the real elapsed weeks.
defects.intended_behaviour: Whole weeks the claim has been open, i.e. FLOOR(DATEDIFF(DAY, reported_date, AsOfDate) / 7).
defects.impact_query: SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_affected, COALESCE(SUM(ABS(weeks_open - CAST(FLOOR(DATEDIFF(as_of_date, reported_date) / 7) AS INT))), 0) AS amount_affected FROM golden_rpt_claim_aging WHERE weeks_open <> CAST(FLOOR(DATEDIFF(as_of_date, reported_date) / 7) AS INT)

impact.query: SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_affected, COALESCE(SUM(ABS(weeks_open - CAST(FLOOR(DATEDIFF(as_of_date, reported_date) / 7) AS INT))), 0) AS amount_affected FROM golden_rpt_claim_aging WHERE weeks_open <> CAST(FLOOR(DATEDIFF(as_of_date, reported_date) / 7) AS INT)

defects.title: A NULL payment amount makes total_paid NULL
defects.description: The cursor builds the total with SET @total = @total + @amount. If any payment up to the reporting date has a NULL amount, the running total becomes NULL and stays NULL, so total_paid is NULL for the whole claim even though its other payments have amounts. The NULL-amount payment is still counted in n_payments.
defects.intended_behaviour: NULL amounts should be ignored (as SUM does), so total_paid is the sum of the known payment amounts.
defects.impact_query: WITH p AS (SELECT claim_id, SUM(amount) AS amt, SUM(CASE WHEN amount IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS n_null FROM stg_claim_payments WHERE payment_date <= DATE'2025-12-31' GROUP BY claim_id) SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_affected, COALESCE(SUM(ABS(COALESCE(p.amt, 0))), 0) AS amount_affected FROM golden_rpt_claim_aging g JOIN p ON p.claim_id = g.claim_id WHERE p.n_null > 0

impact.query: WITH p AS (SELECT claim_id, SUM(amount) AS amt, SUM(CASE WHEN amount IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS n_null FROM stg_claim_payments WHERE payment_date <= DATE'2025-12-31' GROUP BY claim_id) SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_affected, COALESCE(SUM(ABS(COALESCE(p.amt, 0))), 0) AS amount_affected FROM golden_rpt_claim_aging g JOIN p ON p.claim_id = g.claim_id WHERE p.n_null > 0

defects.title: Duplicate staged payment rows are double-counted
defects.description: Payments are copied from stg.claim_payments without removing duplicates (staging has a _row_seq column, which suggests a payment can be loaded more than once). If a payment_id appears more than once for a claim, every copy is added to n_payments and total_paid.
defects.intended_behaviour: Each payment (claim_id, payment_id) should be counted once.
defects.impact_query: WITH d AS (SELECT claim_id, payment_id, COUNT(*) AS c, MAX(amount) AS amt FROM stg_claim_payments WHERE payment_date <= DATE'2025-12-31' GROUP BY claim_id, payment_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1), per AS (SELECT claim_id, SUM((c - 1) * COALESCE(amt, 0)) AS extra FROM d GROUP BY claim_id) SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_affected, COALESCE(SUM(ABS(per.extra)), 0) AS amount_affected FROM golden_rpt_claim_aging g JOIN per ON per.claim_id = g.claim_id

impact.query: WITH d AS (SELECT claim_id, payment_id, COUNT(*) AS c, MAX(amount) AS amt FROM stg_claim_payments WHERE payment_date <= DATE'2025-12-31' GROUP BY claim_id, payment_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1), per AS (SELECT claim_id, SUM((c - 1) * COALESCE(amt, 0)) AS extra FROM d GROUP BY claim_id) SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_affected, COALESCE(SUM(ABS(per.extra)), 0) AS amount_affected FROM golden_rpt_claim_aging g JOIN per ON per.claim_id = g.claim_id

tests.description: Open-book filter with mixed-case status values. Claims 1 and 2 use the canonical 'OPEN' and 'REOPENED'. Claims 3, 4 and 5 hold 'Open', 'reopened' and 'ReOpened'; the case-insensitive collation keeps them in the open book. Claim 6 is 'CLOSED' and is excluded either way. A naive Spark isin(['OPEN','REOPENED']) is case-sensitive, so it would drop claims 3-5 and their payments.

Status values stored with trailing spaces. Claims 1 and 2 are the canonical 'OPEN' and 'REOPENED'. Claims 3, 4 and 5 are 'OPEN ', 'REOPENED  ' and 'OPEN   '. SQL Server ignores trailing spaces when comparing, so it keeps them in the open book. Claim 6 is 'CLOSED ' and is excluded either way. An exact-match filter in Spark would drop claims 3-5.

DATEDIFF semantics on lines 141 and 142, with AsOfDate 2025-12-31 (a Wednesday). Every claim has a non-zero day gap, so a Spark datediff(start, end) with the arguments reversed would give negative days_since_activity and push claims into the wrong band. DATEDIFF(WEEK) counts the Sundays crossed, which differs from floor(days/7) in these claims: claim 1 reported 2025-12-26 (Friday, 5 days, crosses 12-28); claim 2 reported 2025-12-20 (Saturday, 11 days, crosses 12-21 and 12-28); claim 3 reported 2025-12-27 (Saturday, 4 days). Claim 4 is reported on a Sunday, 2025-12-21, and is a control case where both methods agree. Claim 5 (reported 2025-09-06, a Saturday, with payments) and claim 6 (reported 2025-11-29, a Saturday, unpaid) cover longer gaps. Some payments fall after the reporting date and must be ignored.

lineage agent notes: 1) Bug in aging_band (lines 145-148): when days_since_activity = 30 the row falls into 'UNKNOWN', because the bands are <30, 31-60 and >60. The PySpark port must keep this. 2) total_paid is 0, not NULL, when a claim has no payments (@total starts at 0 on line 115), even though the column allows NULL. last_payment_date is NULL in that case. 3) n_payments is a count of payment rows. It is mapped to stg.claim_payments.payment_id plus a constant, with lower confidence. 4) The filters on payment_date, the payment claim_id join and @AsOfDate on line 85 only limit which payments are added up. They don't decide which output rows appear; one row is written per open claim. 5) The final join of #aging to #open_claims (line 175) is a 1:1 match on stg.claims.claim_id. 6) The ORDER BY on payment_date, payment_id decides which payment's date becomes last_payment_date (the last one fetched). The payment_id tie-break doesn't change the value. 7) DATEDIFF(WEEK) counts week boundaries crossed (Sunday-based by default), not elapsed days divided by 7. The port must match this.

translator notes: The two cursor loops are replaced by one aggregation per claim on #pay, which is then left-joined to #open_claims:
- n_payments = count(*), or 0 when a claim has no payments.

Because one output row is built per open claim, this left join stands in for the final #aging-to-#open_claims inner join. It assumes claim_id is unique and not NULL in stg.claims. If it isn't, the legacy job would fail on the #aging primary key, and this port would instead write duplicate rows.

weeks_open is the difference of Sunday-anchored week numbers, using DATE 1899-12-31 (a Sunday) from the TSQL-04 card.

The status filter matches on upper(rtrim(status)), following TSQL-01 and TSQL-02. lob_code is output as UPPER(RTRIM(lob_code)), as in the legacy SELECT.

total_paid is cast to decimal(14,2) inside the job. Under ANSI mode, a total too large for that type raises an error, as the legacy assignment to @total would.
